issues.legal_issue: A conviction based on common intention cannot stand when the accused acted in exercise of the right of private defence.
material_facts: The High Court found that the appellants had acted in private defence but convicted them of culpable homicide with the aid of common intention.
The Supreme Court concluded that the appellants were defending their property and persons, rather than acting with a common intention to commit a criminal act.
issues.conclusion: The conviction for culpable homicide with the aid of common intention was illegal and was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 96 and 103 of the Indian Penal Code, an act done in exercise of the right of private defence is not an offence, and the right to defend property may extend to causing death subject to Section 99. Common intention under Section 34 cannot be attributed to persons acting in exercise of that right. The Court relied on State of Bihar v. Mathu Pandey, which explained that an assertion of a right of private defence within legal limits is not an unlawful common object under Section 141 IPC.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The accused appealed against their criminal convictions.
predicates.acts_done_in_private_defence: The accused acted to defend their property or persons from an attack or intrusion.
predicates.conviction_based_on_common_intention: The conviction rested on attributing a common intention to commit the criminal act.

issues.definition: When accused appealing their convictions acted in private defence, a conviction resting on common intention cannot stand.

issues.legal_issue: Accused in settled possession may use necessary force to defend possession and persons against an intrusion where the circumstances create a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous bodily harm, and the force used in the heat of the moment is not assessed with exacting precision.
material_facts: The appellants had been in continuous possession of the land as cultivating tenants for many years, and the prosecution party had not established settled possession of it.
The prosecution party had attempted to take possession on the previous day, retreated after protest, and returned the next morning to plough the land.
In the ensuing incident, members of both groups were injured; some appellants had injuries to the head, and the prosecution did not explain those injuries.
The High Court found that the appellants were defending their possession, but held that they had exceeded their right of private defence.
The Supreme Court found that the appellants were the persons defending possession and that the circumstances justified a reasonable apprehension of grievous harm or death.
issues.conclusion: The appellants had not exceeded their right of private defence and were entitled to defend their possession and persons; the convictions could not be sustained.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 96 to 106 IPC govern private defence; Section 103 permits the defence of property to extend to causing death in the specified circumstances, subject to Section 99. A person in settled possession may defend that possession even against the rightful owner, while stray or intermittent acts of trespass do not create settled possession. The right is liberally construed, and a person facing imminent peril is not expected to calculate the precise force required. The accused’s burden under Section 105 of the Evidence Act is not as onerous as the prosecution’s burden to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt; unexplained injuries to the accused may support an inference that the prosecution has suppressed the occurrence’s origin or that the defence account is probably true. The Court relied on Munshi Ram v. Delhi Administration, Puran Singh v. State of Punjab, and Mohd. Ramzani v. State of Delhi.

issues.legal_issue: Convictions for injuries inflicted in the same transaction cannot stand when the accused caused those injuries in the lawful exercise of private defence.
material_facts: The appellants had been convicted of offences for causing injuries to prosecution witnesses.
The Supreme Court found that the appellants had acted within their right of private defence and had not exceeded it.
The injuries to the witnesses were caused in the same transaction in which the appellants defended their possession and persons.
issues.conclusion: The convictions for the injury offences could not stand, and the appellants were acquitted of all charges.
issues.legal_principle: Section 96 IPC provides that an act done in the exercise of the right of private defence is not an offence. Once the Court found that the appellants had not exceeded that right, they could not be convicted for injuries caused in the same transaction while exercising it.
